name: OpenDroneMap (ODM)
purpose: Photogrammetry toolkit that turns overlapping aerial or drone images into orthophotos, digital elevation models, point clouds and textured 3D models.
journalism_use_case: Turn drone footage of a site into a measurable orthophoto or 3D model — for example quantifying the volume of an illegal spoil heap, measuring the footprint of unpermitted construction, or producing a to-scale model of a destroyed building for a reconstruction graphic.
pros: Converts footage into measurements, which transforms drone imagery from illustration into evidence — volumes, areas and heights you can state with a stated accuracy
Produces standard outputs (GeoTIFF orthophotos, point clouds) that flow into QGIS for further analysis and into graphics for publication
Actively maintained (v3.6.2, 2026-08-12; pushed 2026-11-13) with a substantial community (6,603 stars) and a well-documented Docker path
Self-hosted, so sensitive site imagery never leaves your infrastructure — unlike commercial photogrammetry services
cons: AGPL-3.0: offering a modified ODM as a network service triggers source obligations, which matters if you build a processing service for partners
Requires properly overlapping imagery with good coverage; footage shot as video or without systematic overlap produces poor or failed reconstructions, and this is the usual reason attempts fail
Computationally heavy — a few hundred images can take hours on a workstation and benefits from substantial RAM; large sets realistically need a server
Measurement accuracy depends on ground control or good GPS metadata, and reporting a measurement without stating its accuracy basis would be indefensible
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 6,603 stars with 126 open issues, release v3.6.2 (2026-08-12), pushed 2026-11-13, AGPL-3.0. ODM is the standard open photogrammetry pipeline, reflected in its adoption in humanitarian mapping (an adjacent field with similar needs).
assessment: Adopt if your work involves drone flights over sites — the measurement capability is a real evidentiary step up from aerial photographs. For your profile two preconditions matter: plan the flight for photogrammetry (systematic overlap, consistent altitude) rather than for pictures, because reconstruction quality is decided at capture; and establish ground control or document the GPS accuracy, since every published measurement needs a stated error basis. Note also the legal dimension — drone flights over sensitive sites carry their own risks independent of this software.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, latest release v3.6.2 (2026-08-12), 6,603 stars, 126 open issues. Regular releases from an established community with a commercial sponsor behind parts of the ecosystem.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Your imagery is yours; derived models inherit whatever rights attach to the source imagery.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified network service built on ODM must publish source. Internal processing is unaffected. Note that WebODM (the web interface) is separately licensed — check it if you deploy that too.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a workstation or server with substantial RAM (16-64GB depending on image count) and hours of CPU per dataset; GPU helps some stages. Assumptions: self-hosted, hundreds of images per dataset.
privacy: Fully local processing, so site imagery stays on your infrastructure — the key advantage over commercial photogrammetry services, which would receive imagery of a site you may be investigating.
alternatives: Commercial photogrammetry services for speed, accepting imagery disclosure
QGIS georeferencing for simpler 2D measurement from a single aerial image
Satellite imagery via pystac where resolution suffices and no flight is possible

name: dump1090 (FlightAware fork)
purpose: Mode S and ADS-B decoder for RTL-SDR software-defined radio receivers, decoding aircraft transponder broadcasts into position, altitude, speed and identity data with a local web map.
journalism_use_case: Independent aircraft tracking from your own receiver: record every aircraft overhead with timestamps, including flights that commercial tracking sites filter, block or do not cover. For reporting on surveillance aircraft, rendition flights or military movements, your own receiver is evidence nobody can retract.
pros: Your own receiver produces your own data, which cannot be blocked, filtered or withdrawn — the decisive advantage over commercial tracking sites that honour blocking requests from aircraft owners
Hardware cost is trivial (an RTL-SDR dongle and an antenna), making this one of the cheapest independent evidence-collection capabilities available to a newsroom

GPL-2.0-or-later (licence resolved in this session; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) with active maintenance (pushed 2026-11-03, tag v11.1) and a maintainer who explicitly invites contact for GPL-incompatible uses
The FlightAware fork is the practically maintained line in a family of forks, so it is the right starting point
cons: Coverage is line-of-sight from your antenna — typically 100-400km in good conditions — so a single receiver sees only its own region, and building wider coverage means recruiting receivers
Aircraft can disable or spoof ADS-B transmission, and military aircraft frequently do, so absence of a track means nothing and presence can be falsified
Requires hardware, an antenna with a reasonable sky view, and some radio literacy — a real setup effort rather than a software install
GitHub reports NOASSERTION so automated licence scanning does not resolve it, and the fork landscape (antirez, MalcolmRobb, FlightAware) confuses newcomers about which to use
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,153 stars with 86 open issues, latest tag v11.1, pushed 2026-11-03, licence resolved by reading the blob to GPL-2.0-or-later with the maintainer inviting contact for GPL-incompatible use. The fork lineage (antirez original, MalcolmRobb last pushed 2024-08-14, FlightAware current) was verified via the API.
assessment: Adopt if aviation is a live beat — the cost is negligible and the independence is the point. For your profile the strongest pattern is a small network: two or three receivers at reporters' homes or offices covering an airport or a flight corridor, feeding a shared store, which gives you coverage a single site cannot. Pair with bellingcat/adsb-history for querying accumulated data, and never treat absence of a track as evidence an aircraft did not fly.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-03, no release objects, latest tag v11.1, SPDX NOASSERTION (GPL-2.0-or-later per the licence blob), 1,153 stars, 86 open issues. Corporate-maintained fork with current commits; by comparison antirez/dump1090 last pushed 2026-02-15 and MalcolmRobb/dump1090 2024-08-14.
licence: GPL-2.0-or-later (licence blob read 2026-11-17 — 'licensed under the GPL, v2 or later', with the maintainer inviting contact for GPL-incompatible uses; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. The ADS-B data you receive is broadcast in the clear; your recordings are your own.
licence_restrictions: GPL-2.0-or-later on the software. Note that receiving and recording broadcast ADS-B is lawful in most jurisdictions but not all — check local radio law before deploying, as this is a legal rather than licence question.
costs: No software fee. Hardware: an RTL-SDR dongle and antenna (tens of dollars/euros each, prices not verified here) plus a small always-on computer such as a Raspberry Pi. Storage grows with traffic volume — modest. Among the best capability-per-cost ratios in this catalogue.
privacy: Entirely local reception and decoding: nothing is transmitted unless you choose to feed an aggregator. Feeding FlightAware or similar networks shares your data and your receiver's location with them — a deliberate choice, and one to decline if your receiver's location should stay private.
alternatives: readsb or tar1090 as modern alternatives in the same ecosystem
bellingcat/adsb-history for querying historical ADS-B without running a receiver
Commercial tracking APIs, which are easier but filterable and withdrawable

name: adsb-history
purpose: Tool to collect and query historical ADS-B aircraft data by geographic region, altitude and time, to identify specific aircraft and movement trends.
journalism_use_case: The analytical layer over aircraft data: find every aircraft that circled a given area below a given altitude over a period — the standard method for identifying surveillance aircraft, which loiter in orbits over neighbourhoods rather than flying point to point.
pros: Implements the specific query that surveillance-aircraft reporting depends on — region plus altitude plus loitering pattern — rather than leaving you to write it
Works against historical data, so you can investigate past activity rather than only watching live, which is what most such stories require
MIT licensed and built by Bellingcat, whose investigators have done substantial published work on surveillance aircraft
Actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-09) and small enough to adapt
cons: Depends on third-party historical ADS-B data sources, whose availability, coverage and terms are outside your control — the data dependency is the real risk, not the code
No releases (100 stars, 8 open issues), so pinning relies on commits and the project is small

Aircraft with disabled or spoofed ADS-B are invisible, and military and some state aircraft routinely are, so this method finds the surveillance aircraft that transmit and systematically misses those that do not
Identifying an aircraft's operator from a registration requires separate research (civil registries, FAA/EASA records), which this does not do
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 100 stars with 8 open issues, no releases, last push 2026-11-09, MIT licence. Bellingcat's published surveillance-aircraft investigations are the relevant context for the technique's effectiveness, though I verified no specific use of this tool.
assessment: Adopt for aviation-related investigation — it encodes a method that would otherwise take you days to work out. For your profile combine it with your own dump1090 receiver where possible, because that gives you a data source nobody can withdraw, and with registry research to get from a tail number to an operator. State clearly in published work that aircraft without ADS-B are invisible to the method, since that limitation is the obvious line of attack on such a story.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-09, no releases or tags, 100 stars, 8 open issues. Recent commits from an institutional maintainer; small project maintained alongside Bellingcat's investigative needs.
model_or_data_licence: Historical ADS-B data comes from third-party sources with their own terms; check the source you configure before republishing raw data.
licence_restrictions: None on the code. Data-source terms are the constraint on redistribution.
costs: No software fee. Historical ADS-B data access may involve paid tiers depending on the source — not priced in this survey. Negligible compute.
privacy: Queries go to whichever historical data source you configure, disclosing the regions and periods you are investigating. Your own receiver data (via dump1090) avoids this entirely.
alternatives: Running your own dump1090 receiver for data nobody can withdraw
Commercial ADS-B history APIs directly, with their own costs and terms
ADSBexchange-style community data, noting access terms vary

name: rtl-ais
purpose: Software-defined-radio AIS receiver that tunes both marine AIS frequencies with an RTL-SDR dongle and decodes vessel position reports to NMEA output.
journalism_use_case: Independent vessel tracking from your own receiver: record AIS broadcasts from ships in range with timestamps, including vessels whose tracks are obscured, delayed or absent from commercial platforms. For reporting on sanctions-evading tankers, illegal fishing or arms shipments, locally received AIS is evidence you hold directly.
pros: Dual-frequency reception in one dongle is the technical point — AIS uses two channels and single-channel receivers miss roughly half the traffic
Your own receiver cannot be filtered or rate-limited, unlike commercial AIS platforms which delay or withhold data for some vessels and regions
Trivial hardware cost (an RTL-SDR and a VHF antenna), making independent maritime monitoring affordable for a small newsroom near a port or strait
GPL licensed (resolved from source headers in this session) and still receiving commits (pushed 2026-08-05)
cons: Coverage is VHF line-of-sight — realistically 20-60km from a coastal antenna — so it monitors a strait or port approach, not an ocean; open-water tracking needs satellite AIS, which is commercial

AIS is self-reported and routinely manipulated: vessels switch off transponders (going dark), spoof positions and transmit false identities, which is itself often the story but means a track is a claim rather than a fact
No releases since v0.3 (2018-08-01) despite recent commits, so versioning signals are weak, and GitHub reports NOASSERTION for the licence
Requires an antenna with sea view and some radio setup; decoding output is NMEA, so you need downstream tooling to make it useful
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 311 stars with 4 open issues, release v0.3 (2018-08-01), last push 2026-08-05, SPDX NOASSERTION with GPL established from source headers (derived from rtl_fm, AISDecoder and GNUAIS lineage, read 2026-11-17).
assessment: Adopt if you have a coastal or strait location and a maritime beat — the independence argument is identical to ADS-B and the hardware cost is just as low. For your profile the realistic framing is that a local receiver documents a chokepoint extremely well and the open ocean not at all, so it complements rather than replaces commercial or satellite AIS. The analytically valuable signal is often the gap: a vessel that goes dark in your coverage area and reappears elsewhere is a documented AIS interruption, which is a reportable fact.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-08-05, latest release v0.3 (2018-08-01), 311 stars, 4 open issues. Commits within the last four months but no release in eight years; a small, functionally complete C tool. Stable rather than dormant given current commits.
licence: GPL (from source headers: derived from rtl_fm by Kyle Keen, AISDecoder by Astra Paging/AISHub and GNUAIS; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Received AIS broadcasts are transmitted in the clear; your recordings are your own.
licence_restrictions: GPL from the upstream lineage. Receiving AIS is lawful in most jurisdictions; confirm local radio law before deploying, as with any SDR receiver.
costs: No software fee. Hardware: RTL-SDR dongle plus a VHF antenna (tens of dollars/euros) and a small always-on computer. Storage is modest. Satellite AIS, if you need open-ocean coverage, is a commercial service not priced here.
privacy: Entirely local reception and decoding; nothing transmitted unless you feed an aggregator. Note that contributing to AISHub or similar networks shares your receiver's location.
alternatives: Global Fishing Watch API for processed vessel-behaviour data over wide areas
Commercial satellite AIS providers for open-ocean coverage, at cost
AISHub community data, noting its contribution requirements

name: Global Fishing Watch API client
purpose: Python client for Global Fishing Watch APIs, providing access to processed vessel-tracking data including apparent fishing effort, vessel identity, port visits, encounters, loitering events and AIS gaps.
journalism_use_case: Maritime investigation at ocean scale: identify vessels that met at sea (encounters), loitered in a protected area, visited a sanctioned port, or went dark for a period — the behavioural events that constitute illegal fishing, sanctions evasion and trans-shipment stories, already extracted from raw AIS.
pros: Provides derived behavioural events — encounters, loitering, AIS gaps, port visits — which is the hard analytical work already done; deriving these from raw AIS yourself is a major project
Global coverage including satellite AIS, so it answers open-ocean questions that a local receiver cannot
Apache-2.0 client with institutional backing from an organisation whose purpose is public-interest transparency, and actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-16)
The AIS-gap detection is directly investigative: a vessel going dark near a sanctioned port is a lead that this data surfaces systematically
cons: Requires an API token and the data terms are Global Fishing Watch's, not an open licence — confirm attribution and redistribution conditions before publishing a derived dataset (terms not verified in this survey)
The derived events are model outputs: 'apparent fishing effort' is inferred from movement patterns and can be wrong, so an event is a lead requiring corroboration rather than a finding
Your queries disclose which vessels and areas you are investigating to GFW — an organisation with a transparency mission, but still a third party
Tiny community (35 stars, 4 open issues) and a modest release cadence (v1.4.0, 2026-01-13), so you will be reading source
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 35 stars with 4 open issues, release v1.4.0 (2026-01-13), pushed 2026-11-16, Apache-2.0 on the client. Global Fishing Watch data has been used in published investigative reporting on illegal fishing, which is relevant context for the data's credibility, though its terms were not verified here.
assessment: Adopt for any maritime investigation — the behavioural-event layer is genuinely hard to reproduce and this is the practical way to get it. For your profile, settle the data terms in writing before you plan to publish a derived dataset, and treat every event as a hypothesis: 'apparent fishing' and 'loitering' are inferences, and the published claim should rest on the vessel's documented behaviour plus corroboration (satellite imagery, port records, company filings), not on the classification alone.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v1.4.0 (2026-01-13), 35 stars, 4 open issues. Current commits with an institutional maintainer that operates the underlying service; small client library tracking an active API.
model_or_data_licence: Global Fishing Watch data terms apply and were NOT verified in this survey — confirm attribution and redistribution conditions before publishing derived data.
licence_restrictions: Client is permissive. The data terms are the unresolved item: GFW publishes data for public-interest use but with its own conditions, which must be read before republication.
costs: Client free. API access requires a token; current access tiers and any limits were NOT verified in this survey — historically available free for research and journalism, which should be confirmed. Negligible compute.
privacy: Queries go to Global Fishing Watch, disclosing the vessels and sea areas you are investigating. GFW's mission is transparency rather than commerce, which lowers but does not remove the concern.
alternatives: rtl-ais for independent local AIS reception in a chokepoint
Commercial satellite AIS providers for raw open-ocean data, at cost
Deriving encounters and gaps yourself from raw AIS — substantially more work
blockers: Data terms and current access tiers not verified — confirm before publishing derived datasets
